    How the experiment worked

    1. Prepare the data. Normalize column names, check missing values, and remove the duplicate record. Keep the binary labels as provided in the project CSV.
    2. Split the data. Use a stratified 80/20 split with random seed 42. Fit preprocessing and models using training records and their cross-validation folds.
    3. Train and tune. Standardize five numeric features and one-hot encode eight categorical features. Compare defaults with a grid search that ranks candidates by mean accuracy across five stratified folds.
    4. Evaluate. Report accuracy, precision, recall, F1 and ROC-AUC on the same 61 held-out records. Logistic regression led test accuracy and shared the best ROC-AUC with the support vector machine.
    5. Explain. Use independent-background Linear SHAP with 50 sampled training records as the reference and 50 sampled test records for the global summaries.

    How to read the results

    Accuracy is the share of correct classifications. Precision is the share of positive predictions that were correct. Recall is the share of positive labels the model found. F1 balances precision and recall. ROC-AUC measures how well scores rank the two classes over different thresholds.

    Limitations

    The study used one small dataset and one held-out split. Ranking models by that split can make the winner's reported performance optimistic. External validation, calibration, and subgroup fairness were outside the study. Some category definitions in the working CSV are undocumented, so the demo displays those values as dataset codes.

    Dataset reference

    The project uses its original 303-row heart.csv. UCI documents the related Cleveland Heart Disease dataset; the exact recoding and provenance of the working CSV were unverified.
